# Scope and Lifetime {.unnumbered}

**Scope** = where the name can be used. **Lifetime** = how long the storage exists. Different questions.

## The table

| Declared | Scope — where the name works | Lifetime — how long the storage lasts |
|---|---|---|
| in a block `{ }` | that block, from the declaration down to the closing brace | until the block ends |
| function parameter | the whole function body | until the function returns |
| outside all functions | every function below it **in that file** — and, with `extern`, other files too | whole program |
| outside all functions, with `static` | every function below it in that file, **and nowhere else** | whole program |
| in a block, with `static` | that block only | **whole program** |

### What each row means

**In a block.** The ordinary case. The name exists from its declaration to the closing brace,
and the storage disappears with it. Declaring the same name in two different blocks creates
two unrelated variables.

**A parameter.** Behaves exactly like a local declared at the top of the function — it just
starts with a copy of the argument.

**Outside all functions — a "global".** This is the row worth reading twice, because its
scope is larger than the file it is written in.

Within the file, every function *below* the declaration can use it. A function written
*above* it cannot, which is why globals are conventionally put at the top.

**And another file can use it too.** The variable has *external linkage*: its name is visible
to the linker, so a second file can declare it with `extern` and then read and write **the
same variable** — not a copy.

```c
/* totals.c  — the definition. This is where the storage lives. */
int total = 0;

/* report.c  — a different file, same variable */
extern int total;                    /* "it exists somewhere; trust me" */
void show(void) { printf("%d\n", total); }
```

```
total seen from the other file = 42
```

Change it in one file and the other file sees the change, because there is only one `total`
in the whole program. That reach is what makes globals risky: the list of code that can
modify one is not bounded by the file you are reading.

**Outside all functions, with `static`.** Same scope inside the file, but the name is **not**
given to the linker, so no other file can reach it even by writing `extern`. Those two files
simply fail to link. This is how you keep a variable or helper function private to one file.

**In a block, with `static`.** The odd one. Scope is unchanged — still only that block — but
the storage now lasts for the whole program, so the value survives between calls.

::: {.callout-note}
`static` means two different things depending on where you write it: *survives between calls*
on a local, *private to this file* at file level. Same word, unrelated jobs.

`static` inside a function changes the **lifetime**, not the scope. For `static`, `extern`,
`register` and `auto` in full — including the one-definition rule — see
[Storage classes](storage-classes.qmd).
:::

## One program, all of it

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int g = 1;                    /* global: whole program            */
static int fileOnly = 2;      /* global, this file only           */

void counter(void){
    static int calls = 0;     /* keeps its value between calls    */
    int fresh = 0;            /* new every call                   */
    calls++; fresh++;
    printf("  calls=%d fresh=%d\n", calls, fresh);
}

int main(void){
    int x = 10;
    printf("g=%d fileOnly=%d x=%d\n", g, fileOnly, x);
    {
        int x = 20;           /* shadows the outer x in this block */
        printf("inner block x=%d\n", x);
    }
    printf("after the block x=%d\n", x);
    counter(); counter(); counter();
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { int t = i * 10; printf("  loop i=%d t=%d\n", i, t); }
    return 0;
}
```

```
g=1 fileOnly=2 x=10
inner block x=20
after the block x=10
  calls=1 fresh=1
  calls=2 fresh=1
  calls=3 fresh=1
  loop i=0 t=0
  loop i=1 t=10
```

| In that output | Because |
|---|---|
| inner `x` is 20, outer still 10 | the inner `int x` is a **second** variable — shadowing |
| `calls` = 1, 2, 3 | `static` — storage survives the return, initialised once |
| `fresh` = 1 every time | ordinary local — created and destroyed each call |
| `i`, `t` | scoped to the loop; using them after it is an error |

## Parameters are copies

```c
void addOne(int n)        { n = n + 1; }     /* changes the copy only */
void reallyAddOne(int *n) { *n = *n + 1; }   /* changes the caller's  */
```

(Two different names — defining `addOne` twice is an error.)

## Traps

### Accidental shadowing

**Shadowing** is declaring a name inside a block when that name already exists outside it.
Both variables exist; the inner one *hides* the outer one for as long as the block lasts.

It is perfectly legal, so nothing complains — and the symptom is a variable that stubbornly
refuses to change:

```c
int count = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    int count = 0;        /* you meant to use the one above */
    count++;
}
printf("%d\n", count);    /* 0 */
```

You wrote `count++` and the number is still 0, because you incremented a different variable
that was destroyed at the closing brace. Nothing was wrong with your loop.

It is called "accidental" because deliberate shadowing is rare; almost every real case is
someone re-declaring a name they had forgotten was already in use. See rule 2 below for the
fix, and note that `-Wall` does not catch it.

### Using a block variable after its block

A variable declared inside braces stops existing at the closing brace — including the braces
of an `if`, a loop, or a bare block.

```c
{
    int t = 5;
}
printf("%d", t);     /* error: use of undeclared identifier 't' */
```

The compiler is clear about it, so this one costs you a minute rather than an afternoon. The
usual cause is a declaration that ended up one level deeper than intended: you declared `t`
inside the loop and want to read it after the loop. The fix is to declare it before the block
and assign inside.

### Returning the address of a local

A local variable's storage is released when the function returns. Its address then refers to
memory that no longer belongs to you.

```c
int *f(void) {
    int local = 5;
    return &local;      /* the storage dies here */
}
```

This is **undefined behaviour** — the standard does not say what happens. It may appear to
work, because the memory has not been reused yet, and then fail when some other call reuses
it. That is what makes it dangerous: it does not fail where the mistake is.

`-Wall` does catch this particular shape:

```
warning: address of stack memory associated with local variable 'local' returned
```

To return something that outlives the function you need storage that is not a local: a
`static`, something the caller passed in, or memory from `malloc` (W13).

### Globals used as a shortcut

Reaching for a global to avoid passing a parameter works, and costs you the ability to find
the bug later: any function in the program can change it, and nothing records which one did.
See rule 4 below.

## Rules of thumb

**1. Declare a variable in the smallest block that needs it.**

If a variable is only used inside a loop, declare it inside the loop. The compiler then
refuses to let you use it anywhere else, which turns a whole class of mistake into an error
you see immediately instead of a wrong answer you have to hunt for.

```c
int total = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {    /* i belongs to the loop        */
    int doubled = a[i] * 2;      /* doubled belongs to one pass  */
    total += doubled;
}
/* using i or doubled here is an error — which is the point */
```

It also keeps the reader's job small: a name declared three lines above is one you can still
see, and one declared at the top of a 60-line function is not.

**2. If the same name appears in nested scopes, rename one of them.**

The inner declaration *shadows* the outer one: both exist, and the name refers to whichever
is nearer. This is legal, so the compiler says nothing, and the symptom is a value that
"refuses to change".

```c
int count = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    int count = 0;        /* a SECOND count — the outer one never moves */
    count++;
}
printf("%d\n", count);    /* prints 0, not n */
```

Rename the inner one (`seen`, `local`, anything) and the bug cannot occur. Note this applies
to function parameters too: a parameter named `count` shadows a global `count` for the whole
function body.

`-Wall -Wextra` does **not** warn about this. The flag that does is `-Wshadow`, and it is not
switched on by default:

```
warning: declaration shadows a local variable [-Wshadow]
```

**3. Use a `static` local only when a value genuinely must survive between calls.**

The legitimate cases are narrow — counting how many times a function has run, remembering a
result that is expensive to recompute, holding a one-time setup flag.

```c
void logLine(char s[]) {
    static int lineNo = 0;       /* survives; numbers the output */
    lineNo++;
    printf("%d: %s\n", lineNo, s);
}
```

The cost is that the function is no longer predictable from its arguments alone: calling it
twice with the same input gives different output. That makes it harder to test and harder to
reason about, so it should be a decision, not a convenience. If the caller could just as
easily pass the value in and get it back, do that instead.

**4. Avoid globals in this course — pass values in and return them out.**

A global is in scope for every function below it, so any of them can change it and nothing
records which one did. When the value is wrong you have no shortlist of suspects, and the
function's signature no longer tells you what it depends on.

```c
int total;                    /* global */
void addTo(int x) { total += x; }     /* what else touches total? you must read everything */

int addTo(int total, int x) { return total + x; }   /* better: it is all in the signature */
```

The exception is a genuine program-wide constant, and for that prefer `#define MAX 100` or
`const`, which cannot be modified by accident.
